s: Marcus sets two cones exactly 10.0 meters apart in an empty, fenced parking lot. A friend films from the side as he rolls past both cones at an easy pace. The video shows 2.5 seconds between them. *Average speed* is distance divided by time: 10.0 m ÷ 2.5 s = 4.0 *meters per second* (m/s). Multiply by 3.6 to get kilometers per hour: 14.4 km/h. The answer stands for the whole stretch, even if he sped up or slowed a little. A shorter *gate* is the measured gap between two marks. Wear a helmet and wrist guards, and the filmer stands well to the side of the path.
m: To get a feel for the numbers, compare them. A relaxed walk is about 1.4 m/s. A very fast sprinter covers 100 meters in about 10 seconds, an average of about 10 m/s. Marcus's 4.0 m/s sits between the two, almost three times a walk. The tape matters too. Pull it straight and tight, because a sagging tape reads longer than the true straight distance between the cones, and then every speed you work out comes out too high.

s: A hand stopwatch is often off by about a fifth of a second because of *reaction time*, the delay between seeing something and moving your thumb. Video avoids that delay. Phones record 30 or 60 *frames per second*, which means 30 or 60 still pictures every second. Step through the clip and note the frame where the front axle meets cone one (112) and where it meets cone two (187). That is 75 frames, and 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5 seconds. One frame at 30 per second lasts about 0.033 s. That is the *resolution* of your clock, the smallest step it can show. At 60 frames per second it is about 0.017 s. Write the frame rate in your notebook.
m: Daylight helps your measurement. The camera gathers light for a short moment during each frame, and a moving board smears across the picture in that moment. In bright sun the moment is shorter, so the axle looks sharper and the frame you pick is easier to defend. Also keep the phone still. A steady backpack or a tripod keeps the cones in the same place on the screen from frame to frame, so you compare the board's motion against the cones and not against the phone's.

s: Where you film from changes what you see. A camera that looks at a cone from an angle can make the board seem to reach it early. This error is called *parallax*. Draw chalk lines at each cone and film from far back, square to the path, to shrink it. Then repeat the test. Marcus's five runs were 2.5, 2.4, 2.6, 2.5 and 2.5 s. The *mean* is the sum divided by the count: 12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5 s. The *range* is the spread from his fastest to his slowest run, here 0.2 s. Report both: about 2.5 s, give or take 0.1 s. If one run is far off, write down what happened and do not quietly delete it. Set your rule for leaving a run out before the test.
m: Repeats also tell you about your own method. If five runs differ by only 0.2 s, your timing is steady. If they swing by a full second, something in the setup keeps changing, such as the push, the starting spot or where you pause the video, and finding it is a result in itself. Scientists often write a number with its spread, like 2.5 ± 0.1 s (read it as 2.5 plus or minus 0.1), so a reader sees at a glance how far to trust it.

s: Measure a slope before you trust a speed test on it. Lay a straight board exactly 1.00 meter long on the path. Lift its low end until a *bubble level* on top reads level, and measure the gap under the lifted end. If the gap is 0.05 m, the path climbs 0.05 m for every 1.00 m across. That is its *rise over run*. As a percent it is the *grade*: 0.05 ÷ 1.00 = 5%. On a gentle slope gravity pulls along it with about g times the grade: 9.8 × 0.05 ≈ 0.49 m/s². Test only on paths closed to cars, on a grade you can already stop on.
m: A grade tells you how steep a path feels. A 1% grade looks almost flat to the eye. In the United States, most accessible ramps are built no steeper than 1 meter of rise for every 12 meters of run, about 8%, so that wheelchair users can roll up them. Slopes matter to every kind of rider. A phone's level app can also read the angle, but checking it once with a board and a ruler shows you where the number comes from.

s: On level ground a rolling board slowly loses speed even when nobody brakes. The wheels squash a little, the bearings rub and air pushes back. The wheel and ground part is called *rolling resistance*. A *coast-down test* measures all these losses together. Cross a start line at a steady speed, find your speed from the video, then stand still and let the board coast to a stop. Measure the distance with the tape. If the board crosses at 4.0 m/s and coasts 40 m, the *deceleration*, how fast it slows, is v² ÷ (2d) = 16 ÷ 80 = 0.20 m/s². Harder wheels, near 99A, usually coast farther on smooth concrete than soft ones near 78A. Change only one thing between tests.
m: Bearings and air are part of the loss too. Dust and grit inside a bearing add drag, which is why skaters clean and oil them. Air matters more as speed rises, because its push grows with the square of the speed: double your speed and the air pushes back about four times as hard. At the slow speeds of a coast-down test, rolling resistance does most of the work. At the bottom of a long hill, air takes a bigger share.

s: Skaters wax ledges so boards slide more easily. You can test it with a *luggage scale*, a hand-held hook scale. Use your own portable ledge or a park that allows wax, since wax makes public benches slippery for others. Put an old deck on the ledge, load it to 5.0 kg and pull slowly with the scale hooked to a truck. Read the scale while the deck slides at a steady pace. Weight is 5.0 × 9.8 = 49 N. A reading of 2.5 kg is a pull of 2.5 × 9.8 = 24.5 N. The *coefficient of friction* is μ = pull ÷ weight = 24.5 ÷ 49 = 0.50. After waxing, an example reading of 1.2 kg gives μ ≈ 0.24. The jerk at the very start is *static friction*, the grip of surfaces not yet moving. It is usually larger than *kinetic friction*, the friction of surfaces already sliding. That is why the steady pull is the one to read.
m: Friction depends on both surfaces. The same deck with the same load gives a different μ on wet concrete, on painted metal and on rough stone. That is why your result belongs to your ledge on that day, and why you write down the surface, the weather and how many slides came before. Notice too that μ has no unit. It is one force divided by another force, so the units cancel and you are left with a plain number.

s: Once you know μ, you can predict how far a board slides. On level ground, kinetic friction slows it by μ times g. The *slide distance* is d = v² ÷ (2μg), where v is the starting speed. Speed is *squared*, which means multiplied by itself, so double the speed and the slide gets four times longer. At 3.0 m/s with μ = 0.50, d = 9.0 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 0.92 m. On fresh wax, μ = 0.24 and d ≈ 1.9 m, about double. To test it safely, shove the loaded deck by hand and film it, then compare the distance with the prediction. Real slides rarely match perfectly. A *model* is a simple rule that stands in for the real thing, and a big miss means something in the setup is different from what you assumed.
m: Notice what the model leaves out. It treats μ as the same all along the slide, but wax wears and spreads as the deck moves. It treats the ledge as perfectly flat, but a slight tilt would help or hinder. A good habit is to list in your notebook two things your model ignores and guess which one matters more. Then the next test can change that one thing alone.

s: *Hang time* is how long the board is off the ground in an ollie. Film from the side at 30 or 60 frames per second. Find the last frame where the tail touches the ground, the moment of *take-off*, and the first frame where a wheel lands. Frame 210 to frame 225 is 15 frames, or 15 ÷ 30 = 0.50 s. In the air the board is in *free fall*: gravity alone acts, so rising and falling take equal time, and the climb takes half the hang time. The height is h = g × t² ÷ 8 = 9.8 × 0.50 × 0.50 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.31 m, about the length of a school ruler. Aim for a clean measurement, not a record: film on flat ground you know, with your helmet buckled.
m: The rule has a reason behind it. The climb takes half the hang time, and a board that falls from rest for a time of t ÷ 2 covers ½ × g × (t ÷ 2)², which simplifies to g × t² ÷ 8. Because time is squared, doubling the hang time makes the height four times greater. An ollie that stays up for only 0.25 s rises about 8 centimeters, while 0.50 s reaches about 31. Small gains in time are big gains in height.

s: Test your prediction with marks. Stick strips of painter's tape on a wall behind the ollie spot, one every 10 centimeters, and pause the clip on the highest frame. Read where the middle of the deck sits. A board at rest already sits about 10 cm off the ground at its middle. That is its *resting height*, and you subtract it. If the deck reaches the 40 cm mark, the *rise* is 40 − 10 = 30 cm, close to the 31 cm predicted from a 0.50 s hang time. One frame matters. At 30 frames per second, 14 frames gives about 0.27 m and 16 gives about 0.35 m, so a miscounted frame shifts the height by about 4 cm. That spread is the *uncertainty*, and filming at 60 frames per second cuts it roughly in half.
m: Writing a result with its uncertainty is honest and useful. "About 31 cm, give or take 4 cm" says more than "31 cm" alone, because it tells a reader which differences count. Two ollies that measure 30 cm and 33 cm do not prove that one was higher, since they sit inside the uncertainty. Two ollies that measure 20 cm and 35 cm probably do differ.

s: A ramp trades height for speed. At the top a rider has *potential energy*, stored by height: mgh. At the bottom it becomes *kinetic energy*, the energy of motion: ½mv². Set them equal and the mass cancels, leaving v = √(2gh). For a drop from the *coping*, the rounded edge at the top of a mini ramp 1.2 m tall, the prediction is √(2 × 9.8 × 1.2) ≈ 4.85 m/s. Riders still learning can roll down a small bank instead. Tape marks 1.0 m apart at the bottom and count frames: 7 frames at 30 frames per second gives about 4.3 m/s. For a 70 kg rider the energy at the top is about 823 *joules* and at the bottom about 647 J, so about 79% showed up as motion. The missing 176 J went to rolling resistance, bearing friction, air drag, sound and the rider's legs.
m: The missing energy did not disappear. The law of conservation of energy says that energy is never destroyed, only changed from one form into another. The wheels, the bearings and the pavement warmed by a tiny amount, the air was pushed aside, and the ramp made sound. Most of the "lost" energy ended as a very small amount of heat that nobody can feel. So the gap between prediction and measurement is not a failure of the physics. It is a way of counting where the energy went.

s: A lab report lets someone else repeat your test. Begin with a question: does wax lower the friction on my ledge? Then write a *hypothesis*, a testable guess with a reason: wax will cut μ about in half because it leaves a slick layer. The *method* lists every step and measurement so a stranger could repeat it: the 5.0 kg load, the luggage scale, three pulls per surface, the place and the date. Results come next: a table of every reading, the mean and the range. The *conclusion* answers the question in a sentence or two and says how sure you are. For example, fresh wax lowered μ from about 0.50 to about 0.24, and the effect faded after twenty slides. Share the report so others can repeat the test. When they get similar numbers, everyone can trust the result more.
m: A report is also a conversation across time. A reader a year from now cannot ask what you meant, so the page has to answer for you. Label the units on every number, date the entry and keep the raw readings even after you have found the mean. Sometimes the result that surprises you is the most valuable one, because it points at something you did not yet understand, and that is where the next question starts.

s: Most public skateparks in the United States start when a group of skaters and parents asks the city for a place to ride. The city's parks department usually builds the park on public land, with money the city council approves. The steps run in order. First, *advocates*, the people pushing for the park, show that there is a need. The city looks at sites and holds public meetings. A *design firm* draws plans and estimates the cost. The council votes to approve and fund it, a *contractor* builds it, and the park opens. All this can take several years. Many paid parks of the late 1970s closed in the early 1980s over insurance costs. Free city parks became common later, as towns worked out *liability*, the question of who is responsible when someone gets hurt.
m: Behind each step is a person with a job. A parks planner on the city staff checks that the site is public land and that a path and lighting can reach it. Engineers study the ground and plan how rainwater will drain away. Neighbors and skaters give their opinions long before anyone digs. The slow pace can feel frustrating, but every step also gives the town a chance to catch a problem while it is still a line on paper and cheap to fix.

s: A *community meeting* is where a park's design really begins. The city or the design firm invites skaters, parents and neighbors. Designers bring printouts of the site, and people point, draw and place sticky dots to vote for the features they want. Young skaters who are too young to vote in elections can shape the park here. Meetings work best after school or on weekends, near the site, so students can come. A *survey*, on paper and online and in the languages the town speaks, reaches people who cannot attend. When neighbors worry about noise or trash, answer with facts, such as where the homes are and when the lights switch off. Then the firm shows a *concept design*, a first rough plan, and people react to it over several rounds.
m: Listening matters as much as showing. A good meeting leader asks open questions, such as "What would make you come back?", writes down every answer and reads a few back before people leave, so everyone can see they were heard. Those notes become a record that the council can read later. It shows that the design came from the community and not from a few loud voices.

s: A skatepark's cost depends mostly on its size and materials. In a worked example, a 1,200-square-meter concrete park at $500 per square meter costs 1,200 × 500 = $600,000 to build. Real prices vary, so a real budget uses local quotes. Design, permits, lighting and paths go on top, along with a *contingency*, money held back for surprises. At 10% each, design and contingency add $60,000 apiece. Money comes from several places. A city's *capital budget*, its plan for long-lasting projects such as parks, often pays the most, and state grants, businesses, clubs and fundraisers fill the gap. The Skatepark Project, founded in 2002 as the Tony Hawk Foundation and renamed in 2020, gives a *grant* and advice to many towns. Plan for yearly upkeep too.
m: Fundraising builds support, and it teaches useful skills. A skate-a-thon, a bake sale or a car wash gives young people a chance to count money, keep a public tally and thank the people who gave. A council member who sees a group raise even a small part of the cost can tell that people will care for the park once it is built. A park the town helped pay for is also a park the town is more likely to look after.

s: The *city council*, the elected group that governs a town, makes the final decision because it controls the budget. A skatepark reaches it as an item on the *agenda*, the meeting's published list of business. During *public comment* people can usually speak for a few minutes. A short, clear talk works best: say who you are, say what you ask for, give two or three facts and say thank you. Council members also weigh risk. Some states, including California, have laws that call skateboarding at a public park a *hazardous recreational activity*. These laws limit a city's responsibility when a rider is hurt, especially when rules like wearing a helmet are posted. A decision may come in steps, so keep showing up politely.
m: Council members often hear many speakers in a single evening, so a talk that is calm, brief and prepared is easy to remember. It helps to practice aloud with a timer, write the key facts on a card and end on the exact request, such as "We ask you to approve the site by the library." Even when the vote does not go your way that night, you have put a clear record on the table of what your community wants, and the next meeting can build on it.

s: A *street plaza* copies the city on purpose: ledges, benches, rails, manual pads, banks and short stairs in an open, flat space. It grew from the street era of the 1990s, when skaters filmed at real plazas and schoolyards, and it gives them a legal place to practice. A *bowl* is a deep, rounded basin with curved walls. Bowls come from the backyard pools skaters rode during the California drought of 1976–77. *Transition* is the word for curved riding surfaces, from small quarter pipes to tall bowls. Many towns choose a *hybrid* park that mixes both styles, with smooth banks that link them. Each area draws different riders, so a hybrid spreads people out and serves more ages and styles. The right mix depends on who will skate there, so count skaters by style at the meetings.
m: Flow matters too. In a well-planned hybrid, a rider can leave a bowl, cross a smooth bank and reach a ledge without stopping or crossing another rider's line, so the whole park feels like one long run. Designers sketch these paths on paper before anything is poured, and they ask local skaters to trace the lines they would ride. If two lines cross at speed on the drawing, the plan can change while changing it is still cheap.

s: Every skilled skater started on a gentle bank. A park built only for advanced riders leaves out children, adults coming back to skating and anyone brand new. A *beginner area* with flat ground, low banks and a small quarter pipe lets people learn without dodging fast riders. Placement matters. Designers think about *lines*, the paths riders take through a park. If the beginner area sits where fast lines cross, collisions follow. Put it to one side, with clear *sightlines* across it, so learners are safer and parents can watch from a bench. Features can step up in size, such as 0.6 m, then 0.9 m, then 1.2 m. Speed at the bottom grows with the square root of height, so doubling the height does not double the speed.
m: A beginner area is also a place to learn how to fall. Falling is part of every skater's first days, and a good design makes it safer, with smooth surfaces and no hard objects sticking up near the low banks. Skaters are taught to crouch low, tuck the chin and roll or slide, rather than catch themselves with a stiff, outstretched arm, which is a common cause of wrist injuries. Wrist guards, knee pads and a helmet protect riders while they practice.

s: Most permanent public parks are poured *concrete*. It lasts for decades and needs little upkeep beyond cleaning and patching. It is quieter than hollow ramps because there is no empty space under the surface to drum. It costs the most up front and cannot be moved once it sets. *Prefabricated* ramps are built in a factory from steel, wood or composite panels. They cost less to start and can be rearranged, but they are louder and wear faster. Crews *trowel* concrete smooth so wheels roll with little resistance. *Drainage* matters too. Puddles leave concrete wet and slippery for days, so slopes carry water to drains.
m: Choosing a material is a choice about sound and about time. A neighbor who hears a boom with every landing is hearing the hollow space inside a ramp, not only the skater. Distance from homes and a solid surface can reduce it, but no design makes rolling wheels silent. Time matters too. A park meant to last for decades may cost less over the years if it is built to need fewer repairs, even when it costs more on opening day.

s: Women have skated since the early sidewalk days. Patti McGee won the women's national title and was on the cover of Life magazine in 1965. Even so, for decades many parks felt like places for boys. The Olympics changed what young riders see. At Tokyo 2020, 13-year-old Momiji Nishiya of Japan won women's street gold. At Paris 2024, Arisa Trew of Australia won women's park and Coco Yoshizawa of Japan won women's street. That kind of *representation*, seeing people like yourself succeed, helps new riders picture themselves skating. Planners can act too. A weekly girls' and women's *skate night*, women coaches, a beginner area away from busy lines, good lighting and clear views help new riders feel welcome. *Inclusion* means planning so everyone can take part, so invite girls and women to design meetings directly.
m: Welcome is made of small things. A rider who arrives alone wants to know where to leave a bag, where to sit and whether anyone will mind a beginner on the bank. A sign that lists beginner hours, a bench within sight of the learning area and a volunteer who says hello can matter as much as any ramp. Riding with another person also makes a first visit easier, which is why a set time that everyone knows about is such a simple way to start.

s: Skateparks are not only for boards. In *WCMX*, short for wheelchair motocross, riders use sturdy wheelchairs on ramps and in bowls. Aaron Fotheringham, a pioneer, landed the first wheelchair backflip in the mid-2000s. *Adaptive* skaters ride in ways that fit their bodies. Some sit on the board, some use a wheelchair, some skate with a prosthetic leg, and some are blind or have low vision and learn a park by sound and touch. A park that welcomes wheelchair riders needs a way in: a smooth, paved path from the sidewalk, an *accessible* entrance with no steps, and gentle ramps up to the decks. Smooth, steady curves and wide flat ground suit wheelchairs well. Ask adaptive riders to review the plans. Planning for access from the first drawing costs far less than adding it later.
m: Access helps far more people than the ones it was first built for. The same step-free path that a wheelchair rider needs also serves a parent with a stroller, a grandparent who walks slowly, a child on a scooter and a worker pushing a cart. It also changes how a space feels, because everyone arrives by the same path and no one has to find a side door. A park planned this way tells every visitor that they were expected.

s: Safe parks are designed, not just posted. Signs ask riders to wear helmets and take turns. Open views across the park allow *passive supervision*, the everyday watching that happens when riders, parents and people walking by can see what is going on. Lighting adds hours in winter. LED lights on a timer that switches off at closing time can light the surfaces evenly without shining into nearby windows. Noise is a common worry for neighbors, and physics helps. Sound spreads out as it travels. In open air, each doubling of distance lowers the level by about 6 *decibels*. If a park measures 80 dB at 10 m, it is about 74 dB at 20 m and 68 dB at 40 m. Designers also place the riding area far from homes, choose concrete and put a *berm* or a building between the park and the houses.
m: The 6 dB rule has a reason behind it. Sound from a small source spreads out in all directions, like a growing bubble. When the distance doubles, the same sound energy covers four times the area, so each part of it is weaker. Because the drop is the same for each doubling, a few extra meters help a lot close to the park and hardly at all far away. That is why the first move of the riding area away from a home does the most good.

s: In 1990, skaters in Portland, Oregon, began pouring concrete under the Burnside Bridge without permission. It was a *DIY* park, short for do it yourself. They shaped it by hand and paid for supplies themselves. Over time the city accepted the park, and Burnside became one of the best-known skateparks in the world. In London, skaters have ridden the *undercroft* beneath the Southbank Centre since the 1970s. When a plan threatened to move them, the Long Live Southbank *campaign* gathered wide support, and an agreement in 2014 kept the space for skating. In 2007, Oliver Percovich founded Skateistan in Kabul, Afghanistan, a skate school that paired skateboarding with classroom lessons. Skaters who show up and care for a space can change how a city sees them. Building without permission is risky, so most towns now invite skaters into the official process.
m: Each story has a lesson for a proposal. Burnside shows that people will look after a place they built with their own hands. Southbank shows that a space can be valued for the community that uses it, not only for the buildings around it. Skateistan shows that a skate space can serve children who have few other places to play. A proposal can borrow all three ideas: invite skaters to help build and care for the park, show who already uses the place, and say what the park will offer besides tricks.

s: A *proposal* is the written case for the park. A strong one fits on a few pages and answers the questions council members will ask: why is a park needed, where will it go, what will it cost and who will pay, and how will it be kept safe and clean? *Evidence* makes the case. Count how many people skate in town with a survey and a sign-in sheet. List where skaters ride now and the problems that causes. Add your own measurements, such as the slope of the site or a sound reading at the nearest home. Ask a nearby park of similar size about its use and upkeep, because facts from a real neighbor carry weight. Attach the drawings, the budget table and each *letter of support* from parents, teachers, police or businesses.
m: A proposal also shows respect. It thanks the people who helped, names the questions the council may still have and says what the group will keep doing after the vote, such as helping with cleanup days or teaching beginners. Council members are asked for many things, and a request that already includes volunteers, numbers and a plan for upkeep is easier to say yes to. It tells them the group will still be there when the park opens.
